front.title: HEART: A HAL Schema Forms Profile for State-Scoped Affordances

abstract.t: This document defines HEART, a profile of HAL Schema Forms for HTTP resources whose legal operations depend on their current state. A HEART representation carries the resource's state and the forms that are legal in that state, and nothing else. Every state-changing request is conditional on the representation the client read. The forms legal in one state are published once, as a shared resource whose bytes the linking representation vouches for with an integrity value, so that many resources and many clients share one cached copy. Refusals are problem details whose types tell a stale request, an illegal one, an invalid one and one refused by a rule apart. The profile is written so that a client, including one whose choices are made by a language model, needs no knowledge of a service beyond its entry URI and this profile.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: A typical HTTP API description lists every operation a server could ever be asked to perform. Which operations are legal for a given resource at a given moment is left to prose, or to the client's own copy of the server's rules. When the server's rules change, every client that copied them must change too, and an operation that has become illegal is discovered by sending it and being refused.

HEART takes the other approach, the one REST describes : the representation of a resource says what may be done to it now. A client binds to operations late, at each response, rather than early, when it is built. A form that a state does not allow is absent, and the server can say why.
HEART adds three things to HAL Schema Forms , a forms extension of HAL whose form bodies are described by JSON Schema :

list.t: Shared affordance sets. The forms legal in a state are the same for every resource in that state, so they are served once, at their own URI, with a long cache lifetime, and linked from each resource with an integrity value.
Conditional acts and distinct refusals. Every state-changing request carries If-Match, and each kind of refusal has its own problem type.
Self-description. Forms are named by link relation types and carry titles and descriptions, so a client, or the reasoner behind it, can understand an act it has never seen before choosing it.

section.name: Notational Conventions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dd.t: A resource's state, with links. Never fresh: it is revalidated on every use.
The forms legal in one state of one resource type. Also Layer 2.
A JSON Schema for a form's body, when it is referenced rather than inlined. Also Layer 3.
The Layer 1 resource whose representation linked to, or embedded, a form.
A request sent by submitting a form whose method is not safe.

section.name: The Profile
section.t: The profile is identified by the URI:

A response that conforms to it names it in a Link header field with relation type profile , beside the parent profile https://w3id.org/heart-rise. The media type is application/hal+json. A client asks for it with Accept: application/hal+json and Accept-Profile: <https://w3id.org/heart-rise/hal-schema-forms>.
A service's entry resource SHOULD link to a machine-readable description of the service with the service-desc relation ; HEART does not depend on it.
The prefix hr: in this document is a HAL CURIE that a server declares in _links.curies, expanding to https://w3id.org/heart-rise/rels/{rel}.

section.name: Rungs
section.t: A client may ask, with the Prefer header field , for less to be inlined:

list.t: With no preference (L0), Layer 1 carries its forms and their schemas inline.
With Prefer: forms=link (L1), Layer 1 links to its affordance set, whose forms carry their schemas inline.
With Prefer: forms=link, schema=link (L2), the affordance set refers to each schema by $ref.

section.t: A server that honours a preference names it in Preference-Applied. A response without Preference-Applied is at L0, whatever its body links to.

section.name: Template Pointers
section.t: A form MAY carry hr:templatePointers, an object whose members map URI Template variable names to JSON Pointers . Each pointer is resolved against the owning resource's JSON body. A client fills each variable from the first of: a pointer for it; a form field of the same name; the owning resource's top-level member of the same name. The value MUST be a string or a number; otherwise the client MUST NOT send the request.
Template pointers let one affordance set serve every resource in a state: the set names no instance, and each client fills the instance in from the resource it read.

section.name: Integrity
section.t: A link MAY carry integrity, and a schema reference MAY carry hr:integrity, in the syntax of Subresource Integrity .
A server MUST send integrity on a Layer 1 link to an affordance set, and hr:integrity on every schema reference in an affordance set. The digest MUST NOT be truncated.

A client fetching a target that has an integrity value MUST hash the body exactly as received and compare it with that value before parsing it. On a mismatch it MUST NOT parse, cache or use the body. A client MUST refuse, before sending any request, a link to an affordance set or a schema reference that has no integrity value.
A client MUST NOT read a digest, or any other meaning, from a URI. The expected digest comes only from the linking representation.
A server SHOULD also send Repr-Digest on affordance sets and schemas. A client SHOULD check it, and MUST NOT require it.

section.name: Schema by Reference
section.t: At L2, a form's schema is an object with a JSON Schema $ref to the schema's URI and an hr:integrity value. The client fetches and checks the schema, then uses it as the form's schema.

section.name: Forms Named by Link Relation
section.t: A form's key in _forms is a link relation type , written as a URI or as a CURIE declared in _links.curies. A client expands a CURIE before comparing names. The relation URI SHOULD identify a descriptor in an ALPS document that says what the act does and when it is offered.

section.name: Self-Description
section.t: Each form in an affordance set MUST carry a title and SHOULD carry a description. Each schema property SHOULD carry title, description and, where it helps, examples. Text in an affordance set MUST NOT include instance identifiers, since the set is shared by every resource in the state.

section.name: Conditional Acts
section.t: Every act MUST carry If-Match with the entity tag of the representation the client read, and repeat the negotiation header fields it read with (, Section 13.1.1). A server MUST refuse an act without If-Match.
A server refuses an act with a problem details object whose type is one of:

texttable.c: Re-read, then send once more with the current validator.
The state has changed since the client read it.
Re-read and decide again. MUST NOT resend the act.
The act is not legal in the current state.
The body breaks the form's schema.
Report each violation. MUST NOT retry.
The body is valid, but a rule of the resource refuses it.
Report the rule's words. MUST NOT retry.

section.t: A 422 problem carries a violations member: an array of objects, each with a JSON Pointer to the offending value and a message.

section.name: Explaining Absence
section.t: An affordance set MAY link, with relation hr:unavailable and an integrity value, to a document listing the acts absent in this state, each with its relation, a title and a short reason. Like the set, it is a function of the state alone and is shared. A client fetches it only when someone asks why an act is missing, and MUST NOT act on any relation it lists.

section.name: Credentials
section.t: A server MAY require credentials on Layer 1 resources and acts, and SHOULD serve affordance sets, schemas and explanations to any caller, since they are the same for every caller. A refusal is 401 with problem type https://w3id.org/heart-rise/problems/not-authenticated and a WWW-Authenticate challenge for each scheme accepted.

A client MUST send a credential only to the origin it is for, MUST NOT send one over unencrypted HTTP beyond the local host, and MUST NOT show a credential to any component that chooses acts, such as a language model. Over CoAP , which has no Authorization option, a service reached beyond the local host SHOULD be reached over DTLS .

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Shared affordance sets are cached for a long time, possibly by shared caches . Integrity values carried by the freshly revalidated Layer 1 are what make it safe for a client to trust bytes it will keep: each layer vouches for the next. A client that skips the check can be given forms that send its acts, and its users' data, anywhere.
Because affordance sets are shared, a server MUST NOT put instance identifiers or per-user data in them. Template pointers are how instance values reach a form, from the resource the client read.
Forms name targets, and a representation chooses where its links lead. A client MUST scope credentials to their origin, so that a link to another origin cannot collect them.

A client whose choices are made by a language model SHOULD give the model only form names, titles, descriptions, schemas and link relations, never URIs, methods, header fields or credentials, and SHOULD check each choice against the representation it holds before sending anything. A model that is never shown a URI cannot invent one.

section.name: Link Relation Types
section.t: IANA is asked to register the following in the "Link Relation Types" registry :

dd.t: Description: Refers to a resource listing the forms (affordances) that are legal in the context resource's current state, shared among resources in that state.
Description: Refers to a resource listing the actions that are not available in the context resource's current state, each with a reason.

section.t: Until these are registered, HEART uses the extension relation types https://w3id.org/heart-rise/rels/forms and https://w3id.org/heart-rise/rels/unavailable, which identify the same relations.

section.name: Profile URIs
section.t: IANA is asked to register https://w3id.org/heart-rise/hal-schema-forms and https://w3id.org/heart-rise in the "Profile URIs" registry , with this document as the reference.

section.name: HTTP Problem Types
section.t: IANA is asked to register the five problem types in the table in the Conditional Acts section, and not-authenticated from the Credentials section, in the "HTTP Problem Types" registry .

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

A URI Template is a compact sequence of characters for describing a range of Uniform Resource Identifiers through variable expansion. This specification defines the URI Template syntax and the process for expanding a URI Template into a URI reference, along with guidelines for the use of URI Templates on the Internet. [STANDARDS-TRACK]
JSON Pointer defines a string syntax for identifying a specific value within a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) document.
This specification defines an HTTP header field that can be used by a client to request that certain behaviors be employed by a server while processing a request.
This document defines a registry for profile URIs to be used in specifications standardizing profiles.
This specification defines a model for the relationships between resources on the Web ("links") and the type of those relationships ("link relation types").
It also defines the serialisation of such links in HTTP headers with the Link header field.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document defines HTTP caches and the associated header fields that control cache behavior or indicate cacheable response messages.
This document obsoletes RFC 7234.
This document defines a "problem detail" to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content to avoid the need to define new error response formats for HTTP APIs.
This document obsoletes RFC 7807.

This document defines HTTP fields that support integrity digests. The Content-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP message content. The Repr-Digest field can be used for the integrity of HTTP representations. Want-Content-Digest and Want-Repr-Digest can be used to indicate a sender's interest and preferences for receiving the respective Integrity fields.
This document obsoletes RFC 3230 and the Digest and Want-Digest HTTP fields.

abstract.t: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) is a specialized web transfer protocol for use with constrained nodes and constrained (e.g., low-power, lossy) networks. The nodes often have 8-bit microcontrollers with small amounts of ROM and RAM, while constrained networks such as IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LoWPANs) often have high packet error rates and a typical throughput of 10s of kbit/s. The protocol is designed for machine- to-machine (M2M) applications such as smart energy and building automation.

CoAP provides a request/response interaction model between application endpoints, supports built-in discovery of services and resources, and includes key concepts of the Web such as URIs and Internet media types. CoAP is designed to easily interface with HTTP for integration with the Web while meeting specialized requirements such as multicast support, very low overhead, and simplicity for constrained environments.

front.title: Link Relation Types for Web Services

abstract.t: Many resources provided on the Web are part of sets of resources that are provided in a context that is managed by one particular service provider. Often, these sets of resources are referred to as "Web services" or "Web APIs". This specification defines link relations that represent relationships from Web services or APIs to resources that provide documentation, descriptions, metadata, or status information for these resources. Documentation is primarily intended for human consumers, whereas descriptions are primarily intended for automated consumers. Metadata provides information about a service's context. This specification also defines a link relation to identify status resources that are used to represent information about service status.

front.title: The Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Protocol Version 1.3

abstract.t: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol. DTLS 1.3 allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.

The DTLS 1.3 protocol is based on the Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 protocol and provides equivalent security guarantees with the exception of order protection / non-replayability. Datagram semantics of the underlying transport are preserved by the DTLS protocol.
This document obsoletes RFC 6347.

section.t: A reference server library (Spring, Kotlin), three domain services built on it, a reference client (ARTIE, Kotlin) with HTTP and CoAP bindings, and a conformance suite exist at https://github.com/JogoShugh/heart-rise-artie. Every identifier this document defines has a page reached through https://w3id.org/heart-rise/.
